newsitem.title: USA: Household "junk" values grow as collectible market booms.
newsitem.headline: Household "junk" values grow as collectible market booms.

text.p: What's your net worth? Add up your bank deposits, IRA, house and car. Don't forget your collectible stamps, china, dolls, old clothing and even Christmas ornaments.
Yes, the collectibles market is booming, and what was junk is now worth a chunk.

"Children. Angels. Christmas. Small-town life. Americans are drawn to collectibles that exert nostalgic, sentimental, or spiritual appeal," according to a report by Packaged Facts, a research and consulting firm based in New York.
"What's more, the appeal is likely to grow with the coming of the millennium and the leap in population of those aged 45 to 64 -- the prime market for collectibles."

The market is growing as baby boomers, bolstered by ample disposable incomes, seek to reclaim childhood memories during a prolonged U.S. economic boom. Rising affluence in Asia also has fuelled demand for indigenous as well as American cultural artifacts such as celebrity memorabilia.

Lest you think your bric-a-brac won't bring you more than supermarket change, the Collectibles & Platemakers Guild and Unity Marketing, a research firm based in Stevens, Pa., reported Wednesday that $9.1 billion in collectibles were sold in 1996, up 11.9 percent from $8.2 billion in 1995.
Sales could hit $12 billion by 2001, Packaged Facts said.

That's just for contemporary items specifically sold as collectibles, such as figurines, dolls and cottage figures. It excludes antiques and unlikely treasures such as old lace, cereal boxes or Coke advertising which have sold for thousands of dollars, for which sales figures are not available.

But judging by auction sales values, boomtime is also here for the "previously junk" category, including mineral rocks, garden ornaments and greeting cards. Collector clubs are mushrooming for anything from porcelain figurines to Star Wars memorabilia to fish decoys. So are trade shows.
But how do you tell the difference between plain household junk and a gold nugget in disguise?

"Virtually anything made by man or woman that is older than 20 years has a high chance of being collectible by anyone. That's not a facetious answer," said Dr. Tony Hyman, who hosts "Trash or Treasure," a telephone radio talk show on about 125 stations on the United Broadcasting Network (http://www.audionet.com/radio/talk/ubn/hyman.htm).

For example, Hyman said one caller asked how much a box of 1960s postcards left by his late father would be worth. It turned out that all the postcards advertised major rock and roll bands and were autographed -- making them worth an estimated $21,000, he said.

"Watch out for costume jewelry and perfume bottles. They turn up in just about any family. You run the risk of giving it away because it's fast and easy, and accept a valuation of $3 per $100," Hyman said.
To find the buyer who will pay the full $100, a seller must enter the market for each category of collectible.

"There are very tiny markets all over the country, the world. Some have 15 people in them. It's not one market," said Hyman. "If want to get most for what any asset you have is, you sell to the person who wants it most."

Hyman's "Trash or Treasury Directory of Buyers" describes "how and where to easily sell collectibles, antiques and other treasures found around your house and neighhorhood" (fax orders to 805-773-8436 or write to Tony Hyman at P.O. Box 3028-R, Pismo Beach, Calif. 93448). It costs $29.95.
Maloney's "Antiques and Collectibles Resource Directory" also lists collectors, clubs, museums, appraisers and periodicals (301-695-8544). The price is $24.95.

Prices depend on rarity, the condition of the item and, of course, demand. While Packaged Facts' report surveyed only new collectibles, it gives an idea of where one can get the best prices for older items because hobbyists tend to want everything they can find in one particular category -- giving secondary prices a boost.
The hottest new collectibles market is in figurines, which accounted for 47.7 percent of U.S. retail sales in 1995, the most recent year for which full data are available, Packaged Facts said.
Dolls followed with 17.5 percent, cottage figures with 10.6 percent, prints 6.3 percent, plush toys 5.2 percent and ornaments with 3.9 percent.
If you want to speculate in this new junk, just keep in mind that prices can drop, as with any investment.

"Collectibles generally appreciate in value if they are popular and limited in number, but that's not true of all of them," said Hunter Haines, executive director of the Collectibles & Platemakers Guild, whose members include Franklin Mint and the Bradford Exchange.
"I never urge people to buy with that (investment) in mind, but to collect for the beauty and interest."
